content.title: About
content.content: Sweet tamales are a traditional Mexican dish consisting of a corn‑maize dough (masa) filled with a sweet mixture of fruits, sugar, cinnamon, and sometimes nuts. The dough is made from masa harina, steamed in small parcels, and then wrapped in corn husks or banana leaves before cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tamales are one of the oldest foods in the Americas, dating back to pre‑Columbian civilizations.
Sweet versions are often served at festivals and Day of the Dead celebrations.
Traditionally the dough is wrapped in corn husks (hojuelas) or banana leaves, which impart a subtle aroma.
Different Mexican regions use various fillings, from pineapple and mango to chocolate and caramel.
Tamales are commonly enjoyed with hot chocolate or spiced coffee.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The corn masa provides slow‑releasing energy, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Corn contributes fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough contains thiamine, niacin, and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants in the filling
items.content: Fruits and spices such as cinnamon are rich in antioxidants that combat free radicals.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Tamales provide magnesium and potassium, which aid muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn‑based products.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet fillings make the dish calorie‑dense; people with diabetes should limit portion size.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: If salt is added to the dough, it may be a concern for those with hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Tamales must be stored and cooked at proper temperatures to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tamales are served hot, unwrapped from their husk. They can be eaten on their own or drizzled with chocolate sauce, caramel, or fruit puree.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked tamales in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a freezer‑safe bag; reheat by steaming or microwaving before serving.
